# Agile Delivery Knowledge Kit

This kit turns delivery practices that usually live in a coach's head into
playbooks, decision guides, and templates any team can pick up on its own.

It is built for distributed teams: several time zones, several holiday
calendars, and a steady stream of requests from other teams.

## Start here

| If you want to... | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Join a new team without disrupting it | [Observe first](getting-started/observe-first.md) |
| Stop confusing story points with days | [Relative estimation](playbooks/relative-estimation.md) |
| Commit to work you can actually finish | [Capacity planning](playbooks/capacity-planning.md) |
| Get help from other teams without scrambling | [Feature Launch Reservations](playbooks/feature-launch-reservations.md) |
| Finish work instead of starting it | [Work in progress limits and swarming](playbooks/wip-limits-and-swarming.md) |
| Run a review stakeholders want to attend | [Sprint reviews](playbooks/sprint-reviews.md) |

## The problem this kit addresses

Teams in this situation often finish only about two thirds of what they commit
to each sprint, and most of that lands in the last two days. That end-of-sprint
spike is called the **hockey stick**.

The causes are usually structural, not personal:

1. Story points treated as days, so estimates become promises about hours.
2. Capacity differences across locations that nobody plans for.
3. Unplanned requests from other teams that never appear in the plan.

Each playbook targets one of those causes.

## How this site is built

Every page is Markdown in Git, checked in CI for broken links, stale content,
and terminology drift, then published automatically. An
[`llms.txt`](https://llmstxt.org/) file packages the content for AI assistants.
See [Contributing](contributing.md) for the full workflow.

---
source: getting-started/observe-first.md
title: Observe first
---

# Observe first

When you are assigned to a new team, resist the urge to roll out practices on
day one. Understand the team before you try to change it.

## The four phases

1. **Observe.** Attend every ceremony and working session for the first few
   weeks. Take notes on how work actually arrives, moves, and finishes.
2. **Help in the here and now.** Remove the blocker in front of the team today.
   Earning trust comes before proposing change.
3. **Ask questions.** Two questions reveal the most:
    - What value does this team create for others?
    - Why does working with this team feel slow to the people who depend on it?
4. **Present gradually.** Share observations first, then evidence, then
   proposed changes. Teams adopt what they help shape.

## What to write down

| Look for | Example signal |
| --- | --- |
| How work arrives | Most requests come as chat messages, not backlog items |
| Where work waits | Reviews sit for days before anyone picks them up |
| Repeated effort | Every request starts from scratch, even standard ones |
| Unowned problems | An issue everyone sees but nobody is assigned to fix |

## Why it works

Jumping straight to "better sprints" can make a reactive team more efficient at
being reactive. Observing first shows you the problem actually worth solving.

## Related

- [Capacity planning](../playbooks/capacity-planning.md)

source: playbooks/relative-estimation.md
title: Relative estimation
---

# Relative estimation

A story point measures how big a piece of work is **compared with other work
the team has done**. It is not a unit of time.

## The common failure

Teams often define "1 point = 1 day." Once that happens:

- Estimates turn into promises about hours.
- People pad estimates to protect themselves.
- Velocity stops being a forecasting tool and becomes a performance score.

## How to estimate relatively

1. Pick two or three **reference stories** the whole team remembers: one small,
   one medium, one large.
2. For each new item, ask "Is this bigger or smaller than the reference?"
3. Use a coarse scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13). Gaps between numbers reflect growing
   uncertainty.
4. Split anything larger than 13 before committing to it.

## Coaching script

When someone says "That's about three days," reply:

> "Compared with the login story we did last month, is it bigger or smaller?"

Redirect to comparison every time. The habit changes within a few sprints.

## Epics and T-shirt sizes

For quarterly planning, size epics with T-shirt sizes (S, M, L, XL) and map each
size to a point range only after the team agrees on reference epics.

## Related

- [Capacity planning](capacity-planning.md) uses velocity built on relative estimates.

---
source: playbooks/capacity-planning.md
title: Capacity planning
---

# Capacity planning

Commit to what the team has **actually** delivered recently, adjusted for who
will be available. Optimism is not a forecast.

## Yesterday's weather

The best predictor of next sprint's velocity is the average of the last three
sprints. This technique is known in the agile community as **yesterday's
weather**.

| Sprint | Completed points |
| --- | --- |
| Sprint 10 | 31 |
| Sprint 11 | 27 |
| Sprint 12 | 32 |
| **Forecast for Sprint 13** | **30** |

## Adjust for availability

Distributed teams lose capacity unevenly. A national holiday in one country can
remove a third of a team for a day while the rest work normally.

1. List each team member's location.
2. Mark that location's public holidays in the sprint.
3. Add planned time off.
4. Compute the **capacity factor**: available person-days divided by normal
   person-days.
5. Multiply the velocity forecast by the capacity factor.

**Example:** 8 people × 10 days = 80 normal person-days. Holidays and time off
remove 12, leaving 68. Capacity factor = 68 / 80 = 0.85. Forecast = 30 × 0.85 ≈ 25 points.

## Best case and worst case

Plan quarters with a range, not a single number:

- **Best case:** the highest of the last three sprints × capacity factor.
- **Worst case:** the lowest of the last three sprints × capacity factor.

Commit to the worst case. Treat anything above it as stretch work.

## Reserve capacity for other teams

If other teams regularly need your help, reserve that time up front with
[Feature Launch Reservations](feature-launch-reservations.md) instead of letting
it erode the plan.

## Related

- [Relative estimation](relative-estimation.md)
- [Work in progress limits and swarming](wip-limits-and-swarming.md)

---
source: playbooks/feature-launch-reservations.md
title: Feature Launch Reservations
---

# Feature Launch Reservations

A **Feature Launch Reservation (FLR)** is a block of time a team books with the
teams it depends on, during quarterly planning, before the quarter starts.

## The analogy

It works like a restaurant reservation. You book the table ahead of time. You do
not need to know what you will order. That part emerges during the meal.

Without a reservation, teams scramble mid-quarter over chat, hoping someone is
available. It is like trying to get a table on a Friday night without calling
ahead.

## What a reservation looks like

> Sprint 2, first two days, 09:30–11:30 on a video call. It is on the calendar
> before the quarter starts.

## How it works

1. During quarterly planning, each team lists the features that depend on
   another team.
2. The teams agree on reservation windows for those launches.
3. During a window, the supporting team joins the call **with work they can
   pick up and put down**.
4. If nothing goes wrong, they keep working on their own items. If something
   unexpected happens, the right people are already together with full context.

## Anticipated pushback

| Objection | Response |
| --- | --- |
| "We already have a chat group for features." | Good. You have the restaurant's number. Now call ahead and book the table. |
| "How can we reserve if we don't know the details yet?" | You don't order your meal when you book a table. You just need to know you'll be hungry. |
| "What if they aren't needed?" | They bring interruptible work. Nothing is wasted. |
| "I'll just reach out to my contact." | Relationships are great, but a favor isn't a plan. What happens when that person is on vacation? |

## When you don't need one

Small configuration changes and low-risk updates can launch without a
reservation. Use the [reservation decision guide](../decision-guides/does-this-need-a-reservation.md).

## Template

Book reservations with the [reservation request template](../reusable-templates/reservation-request.md).

source: playbooks/wip-limits-and-swarming.md
title: WIP limits and swarming
---

# WIP limits and swarming

Stop starting, start finishing. A **work in progress (WIP) limit** caps how many
items the team works on at once.

## Why the hockey stick happens

When each person owns their own items, everything is "in progress" until the
last two days. Then it all closes at once, or doesn't.

## Set a WIP limit

1. Count the people on the team.
2. Set the in-progress limit below that number. For six people, start at four.
3. When the column is full, nobody starts new work. They help finish existing work.

## Swarming

**Swarming** means several people work together on the top item until it is
done. It replaces "my tickets" with "our sprint goal."

- Pair on code and reviews.
- Test while development is still underway.
- Celebrate items finished, not items started.

## Measure it

Track how many items finish in the first half of the sprint. That number should
rise as the hockey stick flattens.

## Related

- [Capacity planning](capacity-planning.md)
- [Sprint reviews](sprint-reviews.md)

source: playbooks/sprint-reviews.md
title: Sprint reviews
---

# Sprint reviews

A sprint review is a working session, not a status report. Stakeholders see
finished work and help decide what comes next.

## Agenda (45 minutes)

1. **Sprint goal and outcome** (5 min): Did we meet it? One sentence.
2. **Demo of finished work** (20 min): Only items that meet the definition of done.
3. **Feedback** (10 min): What should change based on what you saw?
4. **Look ahead** (10 min): Top items for next sprint and any needed
   [Feature Launch Reservations](feature-launch-reservations.md).

## Rules

- Demo working software, not slides.
- The people who built it present it.
- Unfinished work is not demoed. Say so plainly and move on.

## Related

- [Work in progress limits and swarming](wip-limits-and-swarming.md)

source: decision-guides/does-this-need-a-reservation.md
title: Does this launch need a reservation?
---

# Does this launch need a reservation?

Not every launch needs a [Feature Launch Reservation](../playbooks/feature-launch-reservations.md).
Answer three questions.

| Question | If yes |
| --- | --- |
| Does the launch touch a system another team owns? | Lean toward a reservation |
| Would a failure need that team to diagnose it? | Book a reservation |
| Is it a small configuration change with an easy rollback? | Launch and monitor asynchronously |

## Rule of thumb

If you would be messaging another team within an hour of something going wrong,
book the reservation.

---
source: reusable-templates/reservation-request.md
title: Reservation request template
---

# Reservation request template

Copy this into your planning board or calendar invite.

```markdown
## Feature Launch Reservation

- Feature: <name and link to backlog item>
- Requesting team: <team>
- Supporting team: <team>
- Window: Sprint <n>, <dates>, <start>–<end> <time zone>
- Call link: <link>
- Why this team: <system or expertise you may need>
- Rollback plan: <one line>
- Reminder: bring work you can pick up and put down
```

See [Feature Launch Reservations](../playbooks/feature-launch-reservations.md)
for how reservations work.

source: contributing.md
title: Contributing

# Contributing

Every page is Markdown in Git. Changes go through a pull request and must pass
automated checks before they publish.

## Required front matter

```yaml
---
title: Page title
description: One sentence. Used for search, llms.txt, and AI retrieval.
owner: Person accountable for accuracy
last_reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD
review_cycle_days: 180
tags: [topic]
---
```

## Checks run on every pull request

| Check | Command | Fails when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Front matter | `python tools/check_frontmatter.py` | A required field is missing or malformed |
| Freshness | `python tools/check_freshness.py` | A page is past its review cycle |
| Links | `python tools/check_links.py` | An internal link or anchor is broken |
| Terminology | `python tools/check_terms.py` | A discouraged term appears |
| Prose style | Vale | A style rule is violated |
| Retrieval eval | `python tools/eval_retrieval.py` | An eval question doesn't retrieve its expected page |
| Build | `mkdocs build --strict` | MkDocs reports any warning |

Run them all locally with `make check`.

## Writing rules

- Lead with the point. First sentence answers the question.
- One idea per page. Link instead of repeating.
- Define a term the first time you use it.
- Prefer tables for comparisons and numbered lists for steps.

# About this project

Built by **Henry Jones III**, a delivery leader with 25+ years helping
engineering teams ship. The content comes from practices developed while
coaching distributed teams across three continents.

## What this project demonstrates

| Practice | Where to see it |
| --- | --- |
| Docs-as-code | Markdown in Git, pull request workflow, MkDocs |
| CI/CD for content | GitHub Actions: lint, validate, build, publish |
| Content quality automation | Link, freshness, front matter, and terminology checks in `tools/` |
| Prose linting | Vale with a project style and vocabulary |
| AI-ready knowledge | Generated `llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt` |
| Answer-accuracy evaluation | Retrieval eval set in `evals/questions.yml` |
| MCP-accessible source | A small MCP server in `mcp_server/` that serves these docs to AI agents |
| Standards as templates | [Reservation request template](reusable-templates/reservation-request.md) |
| Tribal knowledge to self-service | Every playbook and decision guide |

## Contact

Henry.Jones3rd@gmail.com
